title: Engagement with epilepsy self-management apps: a scoping review to inform clinic support
subtitle: Mapping how engagement is defined, measured, sustained and linked to outcomes
statement: About 40 percent of the clinic's 1,100 adults with epilepsy downloaded a recommended self-management app, but most stopped within weeks and the reports seen at clinic are mostly empty. Before investing nurse time in coaching or building a hospital app, the clinic needs a map of what is known about engagement with epilepsy self-management apps: definitions and measures, levels and duration, features and support linked to sustained use, outcomes linked to engagement, and who does not engage.
whoAffected: Adults with epilepsy, especially older adults, people with intellectual disability and people without smartphones or data; epilepsy nurse specialists and neurologists; the hospital deciding on an app.
whatHurts: Missed doses and unrecorded seizures go unnoticed between visits; nurse time spent promoting an app nobody uses is lost; people without devices are left out of digital support.
currentPractice: Clinicians recommend a free app verbally; nobody follows up on use, and reports are glanced at when patients bring them.
whyNow: The clinic decides on coaching or a hospital-built app in July 2027 and needs the evidence by June.
constraints: No funding beyond clinic time; two screeners for about three hours a week; results by June 2027; research ethics approval already obtained for a linked questionnaire of clinic patients; no patient data leave the hospital.
patientCenteredGoal: People with epilepsy get digital support they can and will use, and no one is left without support because they lack a smartphone.
summary: Problem framed as a mapping question on app engagement to inform a clinic decision.
